bio_ocra.2.0.summary: Cellular respiration is a universal, enzyme-controlled, exothermic metabolic process that occurs continuously in every living cell to release energy from organic molecules. This energy is transferred to synthesize adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the immediate energy currency that drives vital life processes such as active transport, muscle contraction, and protein synthesis. Understanding that respiration is not breathing, but an internal chemical reaction releasing energy, is crucial for securing top marks at GCSE.

core.p: Cellular respiration is a series of enzyme-controlled chemical reactions that happen inside all living cells. Its primary purpose is to break down nutrient molecules, especially glucose, to release chemical energy. This process takes place continuously in every single living cell of plants, animals, and microorganisms.
bullets: Enzyme-controlled metabolic pathway
Occurs inside every living cell
Breaks down organic molecules like glucose
Releases chemical energy continuously

callouts.p: A process involving a series of chemical reactions that takes place in all living cells, releasing energy from glucose.

fig.cap: Overview of cellular respiration in a eukaryotic cell, showing glucose entering the cell and being processed inside to release ATP energy.

core.p: Respiration is described as universal because it happens in all living organisms. Whether an organism is a microscopic bacterium, a giant oak tree, or a human being, every single cell must respire to stay alive and maintain cellular functions.
bullets: Found in all domains of life: Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya
Occurs in every single living cell
Essential for maintaining life processes
Proves common evolutionary ancestry

callouts.p: All living organisms (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria) carry out cellular respiration.

core.p: Cellular respiration is an exothermic process because it transfers energy to the environment, or rather, releases energy from chemical bonds. Although living things use this energy to do work, thermal energy is also released, which helps endothermic animals maintain their body temperature.
bullets: Releases energy from chemical bonds
Transfers thermal energy to surroundings
Contrast with endothermic reactions which absorb energy
Helps maintain body temperature in mammals and birds

callouts.p: A chemical reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, usually in the form of heat.

core.p: Cells cannot use the energy released from glucose directly for every chemical reaction, as this could damage the cell with too much sudden heat. Instead, energy is used to manufacture adenosine triphosphate (ATP). ATP acts as the universal energy currency of the cell.
bullets: Immediate energy currency
Releases energy in small, manageable amounts
Consists of adenosine and three phosphate groups
Readily recyclable into ADP and Pi

callouts.p: ATP is the molecule that delivers energy directly to where it is needed in the cell.

fig.cap: Structure of ATP showing adenosine attached to three phosphate groups via high-energy bonds.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="30" y="90" width="90" height="60" rx="8" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="2"/><text x="75" y="125" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#581c87">Adenosine</text><line x1="120" y1="120" x2="150" y2="120" stroke="#374151" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="170" cy="120" r="16" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170" y="124" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b">P</text><line x1="186" y1="120" x2="216" y2="120" stroke="#374151" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="236" cy="120" r="16" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2"/><text x="236" y="124" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b">P</text><line x1="252" y1="120" x2="282" y2="120" stroke="#374151" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="302" cy="120" r="16" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2"/><text x="302" y="124" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b">P</text><text x="267" y="95" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#b91c1c">High Energy Bond</text></svg>

core.p: ATP is synthesized during respiration by joining adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and an inorganic phosphate (Pi) using energy released from glucose breakdown. When energy is needed for cell work, ATP is broken down back into ADP and Pi, releasing the stored energy instantly.
bullets: Synthesis: ADP + Pi + energy -> ATP
Breakdown: ATP -> ADP + Pi + energy
Catalyzed by specific cellular enzymes
High turnover rate in active cells

callouts.p: Always state that ATP provides energy for *cells*, rather than saying ATP *is* energy.

core.h: Uses of ATP in Living Organisms
core.p: The ATP produced during respiration is vital for powering various biological processes. Without a constant supply of ATP, cells would rapidly die as essential chemical reactions and transport mechanisms would halt.
bullets: Active transport of molecules against concentration gradients
Muscle contraction for movement
Synthesis of large molecules (proteins, DNA, lipids)
Maintaining body temperature in endotherms

callouts.p: ATP powers active transport, muscle contraction, and biosynthesis.

core.p: Respiration is a major part of metabolism. Metabolism is defined as the sum of all the chemical reactions that happen in an organism or cell. Respiration specifically includes catabolic reactions, where large molecules are broken down into smaller ones.
bullets: Metabolism = sum of all chemical reactions
Catabolic reactions release energy (respiration)
Anabolic reactions consume energy (protein synthesis)
Controlled entirely by enzymes

callouts.p: The sum of all the chemical reactions that take place in a cell or in the body of an organism.

core.p: While glycolysis (the first stage) occurs in the cytoplasm, the majority of ATP production in aerobic respiration takes place inside specialized organelles called mitochondria. Cells with high energy demands, such as muscle cells and sperm cells, contain many mitochondria.
bullets: Cytoplasm: initial glucose breakdown
Mitochondria: aerobic stages and bulk ATP synthesis
Mitochondria have folded inner membranes (cristae)
Folded cristae provide large surface area for enzymes

callouts.p: Do not write 'powerhouse of the cell' in exams without explaining that it produces ATP via aerobic respiration.

fig.cap: Structure of a mitochondrion showing outer membrane, inner membrane folds (cristae), and matrix.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><ellipse cx="200" cy="120" rx="150" ry="80" fill="#fef08a" stroke="#a16207" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 80,120 Q 110,60 140,120 T 200,120 T 260,120 T 320,120" fill="none" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M 100,150 Q 130,190 160,150 T 220,150 T 280,150" fill="none" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="3"/><text x="200" y="45" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#713f12">Outer Membrane</text><text x="200" y="215" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#713f12">Cristae (Inner Membrane Folds)</text></svg>

core.p: Students frequently confuse respiration with breathing (ventilation). Breathing is simply the mechanical movement of air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is a chemical reaction occurring inside cells to release energy.
bullets: Breathing: physical movement of air
Respiration: chemical reaction inside cells
Breathing provides oxygen for aerobic respiration
Respiration occurs in all living cells, not just lungs

callouts.p: Breathing is not respiration! Breathing is ventilation of the lungs.

core.p: Every step of cellular respiration is regulated by specific biological catalysts called enzymes. Because enzymes are proteins, respiration rates are heavily affected by temperature and pH changes.
bullets: Enzymes lower activation energy
Specific enzymes for each step
Optimal temperature required
Denaturation stops respiration at high temperatures

callouts.p: Respiration is controlled by enzymes, making it sensitive to temperature and pH.

analogy.t: The Mobile Phone Battery and Charger Analogy
analogy.p: Think of glucose as a large coal power station that contains vast amounts of stored energy. Because you cannot plug your mobile phone directly into a power station without destroying it, the power station charges up portable batteries (ATP). These ATP batteries can then be carried around the cell to power individual apps and functions (muscle contraction, active transport). Where this breaks down: ATP is not stored long-term like a real battery; it is consumed almost instantly after being made.

terms.d: An exothermic reaction supplying ATP, taking place continuously in all living cells.
A chemical reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings.
Adenosine triphosphate, the immediate energy currency of cells.
The sum of all the chemical reactions in a cell or organism.
Organelles where aerobic respiration and bulk ATP synthesis occur.
The jelly-like substance where glycolysis and general metabolic reactions occur.
Movement of particles against a concentration gradient, requiring ATP.
A biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions in cells.
Adenosine diphosphate, formed when ATP releases its energy.
A phosphate group (Pi) joined with ADP to form ATP.
Reactions that break down large molecules into smaller ones, releasing energy.
Reactions that build up larger molecules from smaller ones, requiring energy.
Requiring oxygen to proceed.
Proceeding in the absence of oxygen.
The mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs (breathing).

mistakes.w: Respiration is breathing in oxygen and breathing out carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: Respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells that releases energy from glucose.
Respiration releases energy from glucose to synthesize ATP; energy cannot be created.

mistakes.w: ATP stands for adenosine tri-phosphate energy.
Plants do not respire, they only do photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: Plants respire 24 hours a day in every living cell.

mistakes.w: Mitochondria are the energy of the cell.
mistakes.r: Mitochondria are organelles where aerobic respiration takes place to produce ATP.

mistakes.w: Exothermic means it absorbs heat from the surroundings.
mistakes.r: Exothermic means it transfers energy (heat) to the surroundings.

mistakes.w: Respiration only happens in animal muscles.
mistakes.r: Respiration is universal; it happens in all living cells of all organisms.

model: A chemical reaction/process
that takes place in all living cells to release energy (from glucose)
exam.tip: Mention both that it is a chemical reaction and that it releases energy.

exam.q: Explain why cellular respiration is classified as an exothermic process.
model: It transfers energy
to the surroundings (environment)
exam.tip: Use the exact term 'transfers energy' for full marks.

exam.q: Name the molecule that acts as the immediate energy currency of cells.
model: ATP / Adenosine triphosphate
exam.tip: Write the full name or accepted abbreviation (ATP).

exam.q: Give two uses of ATP in a mammalian cell.
model: Muscle contraction (1)
Active transport (1) (accept protein synthesis / maintaining body temperature)
exam.tip: Learn at least three clear uses of ATP.

exam.q: Explain the difference between breathing and respiration.
model: Breathing is the physical/mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs (1)
Whereas respiration is a chemical reaction occurring inside cells (1)
to release energy / make ATP (1)
exam.tip: Contrast the physical nature of breathing with the chemical nature of respiration.

exam.q: State where in the cell the majority of ATP is produced during aerobic respiration.
model: Mitochondria / mitochondrion
exam.tip: Check spelling: mitochondria is plural, mitochondrion is singular.

exam.q: Describe what happens to ATP when energy is released for cellular work.
model: ATP is broken down
into ADP and an inorganic phosphate (Pi) releasing energy

exam.q: Explain why cells with high energy demands, such as active muscle cells, contain large numbers of mitochondria.
model: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration (1)
which produces ATP (1)
needed to power muscle contraction / active transport (1)
exam.tip: Link mitochondria to ATP production and muscle function.

model: The sum of all
the chemical reactions in a cell or the body
exam.tip: Learn this exact definition word for word.

worked.q: A student measures the temperature change in a flask containing germinating peas over 24 hours. The temperature increases by 3.5 degrees Celsius. Explain why the temperature increased.
steps: Identify the biological process occurring in the germinating peas: cellular respiration.
Recognize that cellular respiration is an exothermic process.
Conclude that heat energy was released into the surroundings, causing the temperature rise.
worked.ans: The germinating peas carried out cellular respiration. Respiration is an exothermic process which releases energy (thermal energy) into the surroundings, causing the temperature in the flask to rise.

worked.q: During vigorous exercise, muscle cells require a continuous supply of ATP. Describe how ATP is synthesized from ADP in the cell.
steps: Identify the components needed for ATP synthesis: ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi).
State the source of energy required: energy released from the breakdown of glucose during respiration.
Combine these points to show ADP + Pi + energy -> ATP.
worked.ans: ATP is synthesized by joining adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and an inorganic phosphate (Pi) together, using the energy released from the breakdown of glucose during cellular respiration.

bio_ocra.2.1.summary: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to completely break down glucose, yielding up to 38 ATP per molecule, while anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is unavailable, producing far less ATP and different end‑products in plants, fungi and animals. Both processes start with glycolysis in the cytoplasm, but the subsequent pathways diverge, giving distinct energy yields and waste products that are crucial for understanding metabolism and adaptations.

core.p: Respiration is the set of metabolic pathways that convert biochemical energy from nutrients into ATP. **Aerobic respiration** requires O₂ and proceeds through glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. **Anaerobic respiration** (fermentation) occurs without O₂ and ends after glycolysis, producing different end‑products in different kingdoms.
bullets: Aerobic: glucose + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + up to 38 ATP
Anaerobic (fermentation): glucose → pyruvate → end‑product + 2 ATP
All organisms perform glycolysis – a universal, exothermic process

callouts.p: A series of metabolic reactions that use oxygen to completely oxidise glucose to carbon dioxide and water, producing a large amount of ATP.
Metabolic pathways that regenerate NAD⁺ from NADH without oxygen, allowing glycolysis to continue, producing far less ATP and characteristic end‑products.

core.p: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of plant, fungal and animal cells. One molecule of glucose (6‑C) is split into two molecules of pyruvate (3‑C).
bullets: Consumes 2 ATP, produces 4 ATP → net gain **2 ATP**
Produces 2 NADH (used later in aerobic respiration)
Key enzymes: hexokinase, phosphofructokinase (PFK), pyruvate kinase

callouts.p: PFK is the main regulatory step – inhibited by ATP, activated by ADP.

fig.cap: Glycolysis pathway showing substrates, enzymes and ATP/NADH yields.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Glucose</text><text x="80" y="30" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">→ 2 Pyruvate</text><text x="20" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">-2 ATP</text><text x="20" y="100" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">+4 ATP</text><text x="20" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Net +2 ATP</text><text x="20" y="160" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">+2 NADH</text></svg>

core.p: After glycolysis, pyruvate enters mitochondria where it is converted to acetyl‑CoA (link reaction), then oxidised in the Krebs cycle and finally used in oxidative phosphorylation.
bullets: Link reaction: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → Acetyl‑CoA + CO₂ + NADH
Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle): each acetyl‑CoA yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (≈ ATP) and 2 CO₂
Oxidative phosphorylation: NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the electron transport chain (ETC) → proton gradient → ATP synthase produces ~34 ATP

callouts.p: Remember the total ATP from aerobic respiration is **38** (2+2+34). Some textbooks quote 36 when accounting for transport costs.

core.h: 4. Anaerobic Respiration in Animals (Lactic Acid Fermentation)
core.p: When oxygen is scarce (e.g., intense exercise), animal muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
bullets: Pyruvate + NADH → Lactate + NAD⁺ (catalysed by lactate dehydrogenase)
Net ATP from glycolysis only – **2 ATP per glucose**
Lactate accumulates → muscle fatigue; later transported to liver for gluconeogenesis (Cori cycle)

callouts.p: Do NOT confuse lactic acid fermentation with alcoholic fermentation – the end‑product differs.

fig.cap: Lactic acid fermentation pathway in animal muscle.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Glucose → 2 Pyruvate</text><text x="20" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">+2 ATP (glycolysis)</text><text x="20" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Pyruvate + NADH → Lactate + NAD⁺</text></svg>

core.p: Fungi such as yeast convert pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂, a process exploited in bread making and brewing.
bullets: Pyruvate → Acetaldehyde + CO₂ (pyruvate decarboxylase)
Acetaldehyde + NADH → Ethanol + NAD⁺ (alcohol dehydrogenase)
Net ATP = **2 ATP per glucose** (from glycolysis only)
CO₂ production causes bread to rise; ethanol is the alcohol in beer/wine

callouts.p: Alcoholic fermentation is the only respiration type that produces a gas (CO₂) as a waste product.

fig.cap: Alcoholic fermentation in yeast – steps and products.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Glucose → 2 Pyruvate</text><text x="20" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Pyruvate → Acetaldehyde + CO₂</text><text x="20" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Acetaldehyde + NADH → Ethanol + NAD⁺</text></svg>

core.p: Plants also ferment when oxygen is limited (e.g., water‑logged soils). The pathway mirrors that of yeast, producing ethanol and CO₂.
bullets: Occurs in the cytoplasm of root cells under hypoxic conditions
Same enzymes as yeast – pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase
Provides only 2 ATP per glucose, sufficient for short‑term survival

callouts.p: In exam questions, always state that the plant pathway is **alcoholic fermentation**, not lactic.

core.p: The three major groups produce distinct waste molecules after glycolysis.
bullets: Animals (muscle) – **lactate**
Fungi (yeast) – **ethanol + CO₂**
Plants – **ethanol + CO₂** (same as yeast)

core.h: 8. Why Aerobic Respiration Yields More ATP
core.p: Oxidative phosphorylation uses the energy of electrons from NADH/FADH₂ to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, creating a chemiosmotic gradient.
bullets: Each NADH → ~3 ATP; each FADH₂ → ~2 ATP
Proton motive force drives ATP synthase (ADP + Pi → ATP)
O₂ is the final electron acceptor, forming H₂O

callouts.p: The **electron transport chain** is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

fig.cap: Chemiosmotic theory – proton gradient and ATP synthase.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">ETC pumps H⁺ out</text><text x="20" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">H⁺ gradient</text><text x="20" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">ATP synthase uses H⁺ flow → ATP</text></svg>

core.p: Key OCR practicals demonstrate the different end‑products.
bullets: Lactate test – add FeSO₄ to muscle extract; a brown precipitate indicates lactate.
Ethanol test – add potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇) in H₂SO₄; colour change from orange to green shows ethanol oxidation.
CO₂ detection – limewater turns milky when CO₂ is bubbled through (used for yeast fermentation).

callouts.p: Do not confuse the ethanol test with the alcohol flame test – the former is a chemical oxidation test.

core.p: Organisms that frequently experience low O₂ have specialised adaptations.
bullets: Plants – aerenchyma tissue in roots and stems to transport O₂ from shoots.
Fungi – can switch rapidly between aerobic respiration and fermentation.
Animals – fast‑twitch muscle fibres rely heavily on lactic fermentation for short bursts of activity.

core.h: 11. Higher‑Tier Extension: Fermentation in Food Production
core.p: Understanding fermentation allows explanation of real‑world applications, a higher‑tier requirement.
bullets: Bread – CO₂ from yeast fermentation inflates dough; ethanol evaporates during baking.
Alcoholic drinks – ethanol concentration depends on yeast strain and fermentation time.
Sauerkraut – lactic acid bacteria ferment sugars to lactic acid, preserving the cabbage.

callouts.p: When answering, link the end‑product to its practical effect (e.g., CO₂ → dough rise).

core.p: A concise table helps recall the ATP yields for each respiration type across kingdoms.

analogy.t: Cellular respiration is like a power plant.
analogy.p: Glucose is the fuel, glycolysis is the coal‑crushing plant that prepares the fuel, the mitochondrion is the main generator where the link reaction and Krebs cycle are the boilers that turn fuel into steam, and the electron transport chain is the turbine that finally produces electricity (ATP). The analogy breaks down because a real power plant does not recycle NAD⁺ and does not produce waste gases like CO₂ and ethanol in the same way as cells.

terms.d: A set of metabolic pathways that use oxygen to completely oxidise glucose to CO₂ and H₂O, producing up to 38 ATP per glucose molecule.
Metabolic pathways that occur without oxygen, ending after glycolysis and producing limited ATP and characteristic end‑products such as lactate or ethanol.
The cytoplasmic breakdown of one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules, yielding a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, producing CO₂ and NADH.
A series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix that oxidise acetyl‑CoA, producing NADH, FADH₂, GTP (ATP) and CO₂.
ATP synthesis driven by the proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Anaerobic pathway in animal muscle where pyruvate is reduced to lactate, regenerating NAD⁺.
Anaerobic pathway in yeast and some plant cells where pyruvate is converted to ethanol and CO₂.
A series of membrane‑bound proteins that transfer electrons from NADH/FADH₂ to O₂, pumping protons to create a gradient.
Enzyme complex that synthesises ATP as protons flow back into the mitochondrial matrix through it.
Spongy tissue in aquatic plants that allows diffusion of O₂ to submerged roots.
The metabolic pathway that transports lactate from muscle to liver, where it is converted back to glucose.

mistakes.r: Anaerobic (fermentation) only yields 2 ATP per glucose; the 38 ATP figure applies to aerobic respiration.
Plants can also undergo alcoholic fermentation when O₂ is limited, e.g., in water‑logged roots.
Yeast produces ethanol and CO₂; lactate is produced by animal muscle cells.

mistakes.w: The link reaction occurs in the cytoplasm
mistakes.r: The link reaction takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
Each FADH₂ yields about 2 ATP in oxidative phosphorylation.
Fermentation is defined by the *absence* of oxygen; it regenerates NAD⁺ without O₂.

mistakes.w: All NADH from glycolysis enters the mitochondria directly
mistakes.r: In animal cells, cytoplasmic NADH transfers its electrons to mitochondrial carriers via shuttle systems (e.g., malate‑aspartate).

exam.q: State the overall equation for aerobic respiration in animals and write down the net ATP yield.
model: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O
Net ATP = 38 (or 36 if transport costs are considered)
exam.tip: Write the balanced equation first, then the ATP total – remember to mention the possible 36/38 variation.

exam.q: Explain why anaerobic respiration produces far less ATP than aerobic respiration.
model: Both start with glycolysis, which yields only 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
In aerobic respiration the NADH and FADH₂ enter the electron transport chain, producing ~34 ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.
In anaerobic respiration the NADH is re‑oxidised in fermentation, so no oxidative phosphorylation occurs.
Therefore only the 2 ATP from glycolysis are produced.
exam.tip: Structure answer: start with common step, then contrast the presence/absence of ETC.

exam.q: Write the equation for alcoholic fermentation in yeast and name the two end‑products.
model: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂
End‑products: ethanol and carbon dioxide
exam.tip: Remember to include the stoichiometry – two molecules of each product per glucose.

exam.q: A plant root is flooded and cannot obtain oxygen. Describe the metabolic pathway it will use to obtain ATP and state the amount of ATP produced per glucose.
model: The root will use alcoholic fermentation.
Glucose → 2 pyruvate (glycolysis) → ethanol + CO₂ (fermentation).
Net ATP = 2 per glucose.
exam.tip: Specify that the pathway occurs in the cytoplasm and that only glycolysis yields ATP.

exam.q: Compare the end‑products of anaerobic respiration in animal muscle and in yeast, stating why they differ.
model: Animal muscle: lactate (lactic acid fermentation).
Yeast: ethanol and CO₂ (alcoholic fermentation).
Difference due to the enzymes present – lactate dehydrogenase in muscle vs pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase in yeast.
exam.tip: Link the enzyme difference directly to the product difference.

exam.q: Explain how the electron transport chain generates ATP in aerobic respiration.
model: Electrons from NADH/FADH₂ are passed through a series of membrane proteins.
Energy released pumps H⁺ from the matrix to the inter‑membrane space, creating a proton gradient.
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, driving the synthesis of ATP from ADP + Pi.
O₂ acts as the final electron acceptor, forming H₂O.
exam.tip: Use the term ‘chemiosmotic gradient’ and mention the location – inner mitochondrial membrane.

exam.q: A student claims that fermentation in plants produces lactic acid. Using knowledge of the OCR specification, evaluate this claim.
model: The claim is incorrect – plants perform alcoholic fermentation, not lactic.
Evidence: plant roots under anaerobic conditions produce ethanol and CO₂, the same as yeast.
Lactic acid fermentation is characteristic of animal muscle cells.
exam.tip: State the correct pathway and give a brief reason.

exam.q: List three adaptations that allow organisms to survive in low‑oxygen environments.
model: Aerenchyma tissue in aquatic plants
Ability to switch to fermentation (yeast)
Fast‑twitch muscle fibres relying on lactic fermentation
exam.tip: One point per line – keep it concise.

exam.q: During a practical, a student adds FeSO₄ to a muscle extract and observes a brown precipitate. What does this indicate and why?
model: Presence of lactate – Fe²⁺ reacts with lactate to form a brown Fe‑lactate precipitate.
exam.tip: Link the test directly to the end‑product of lactic fermentation.

worked.q: Calculate the total ATP yield from one molecule of glucose undergoing aerobic respiration in an animal cell, assuming each NADH from glycolysis yields 2 ATP (shuttle cost) and each FADH₂ yields 2 ATP.
steps: Krebs cycle: 6 NADH → 6 × 3 = 18 ATP; 2 FADH₂ → 2 × 2 = 4 ATP; 2 GTP → 2 ATP
worked.ans: 36 ATP (some textbooks state 38 ATP if the glycolytic NADH yields 3 ATP).

worked.q: Write the complete set of equations for lactic acid fermentation in animal muscle, starting from glucose.
